In a conversation I had with one of the Motamem members under one of the complex systems courses (in the emergence course), I needed to refer to and cite Damasio's new book titled "Natural Intelligence and the Logic of Consciousness." It came out three or four days ago. For those who wonder how concepts like "self" and "identity" take shape in living beings (and more than anything in humans), it offers fascinating answers. This debate is still an unfinished one in the world and will probably never be settled (because it is more a debate in the realm of language and words than in the physical world). But engaging with this debate and its surrounding discussions bears much fruit. I used to introduce Damasio's book Descartes' Error in my in-person classes and teach parts of it. But later, I don't know why, no opportunity came up to mention it in my writings. Damasio, compared to his peers (of whom there aren't many), is not as recognized in our country as he deserves. Perhaps his new book will create an opportunity for him to be discussed more.

National Wealth Fund

This Oxford Handbook on sovereign wealth funds has gotten a bit dated (2017). Especially in the financial and investment industry, which has seen rapid changes. But its structure, the framework it offers, and the points it makes about the architecture of sovereign wealth funds are truly excellent.

You probably know that one of the most famous funds belongs to Norway, where the government saves and invests oil revenues through a mechanism. They call it an intergenerational perspective. Their government says the state has no right to spend oil money recklessly, because it also belongs to future generations.

They started thirty years ago. Now it's around 2,400 billion dollars. That's roughly half a million dollars per Norwegian.

Interestingly, nearly 70 percent of this money is the returns generated by the oil money itself that have been added to the fund. In one chapter of this book, it examines this fund's policies, which was interesting. One of them is that they never take more than a 10% stake (with voting rights) in any company, so they don't have to get involved in the day-to-day affairs of companies. It should just be an investment and they take their money.

From this perspective, they differ from approaches like Saudi Arabia's (PIF), which uses national money to buy large stakes in companies.

Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @bamotamem

On the facade of the main building of the US Post Office in New York (the Farley Building), a sentence is engraved that you may have seen before in photos: "Neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift completion of their appointed rounds." The sentence was engraved in 1914 and is so famous that many consider it the official motto of the US Postal Service. In his book "Neither Snow Nor Rain," which is dedicated to the history of the US Postal Service, David Leonard tells the story behind this sentence. The sentence was used by Herodotus in his famous book, Histories, to describe the Iranian couriers during the era of Darius the Great. The Iranian postal industry began during the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great and reached its peak during the era of Darius the Great, and was known as the fastest organized postal system in the world (the Egyptians and Chinese also had postal systems, but the symbol of fast and organized mail was Iran). Leonard ends the story of how this sentence was chosen and engraved as follows: Many think this sentence is the motto of the US Postal Service. But this sentence is merely the homage of the world's greatest postal system to one of its most renowned ancestors. #هایلایت
